summary.text: For every \(1\le d\le2025\), \(d\) is coprime to at least one of \(2\cdot73,3\cdot47,5\cdot29,7\cdot19,11\cdot13\): otherwise it would contain one prime from each disjoint pair and hence be at least \(2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11=2310\). For such a coprime product \(pq<150\), the progression visits \(0\pmod{pq}\) within its first \(pq\) terms, producing a term divisible by primes \(p,q\) with different final digits, a contradiction.

full_proof.text:
Call an integer greater than 1 lopsided if all of its prime divisors have the same residue modulo 10. We prove that there cannot be integers \(a,d\) with
\[
a\ge 2,\qquad 1\le d\le 2025,
\]
such that all 150 integers
\[
a,a+d,a+2d,\ldots,a+149d
\]
are lopsided.

We first record a standard fact about arithmetic progressions modulo an integer.

**Modular hitting lemma.** If \(m\ge 1\) and \(\gcd(d,m)=1\), then for every integer \(a\) there is an integer \(i\) with
\[
0\le i<m
\]
such that
\[
m\mid a+id.
\]

Indeed, since \(d\) is invertible modulo \(m\), choose an inverse \(u\), so that \(du\equiv 1\pmod m\). Take \(i\) to be the unique representative in \(\{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}\) of the residue \(-au\pmod m\). Then
\[
a+id\equiv a-au d\equiv a-a\equiv 0\pmod m.
\]
This proves the lemma.

Now consider the following five pairs of primes:
\[
(2,73),\qquad (3,47),\qquad (5,29),\qquad (7,19),\qquad (11,13).
\]
Their products are
\[
2\cdot73=146,
\quad 3\cdot47=141,
\quad 5\cdot29=145,
\quad 7\cdot19=133,
\quad 11\cdot13=143.
\]
In particular, every one of these products is at most 150. Moreover, within each pair the two primes have different final decimal digits:
\[
2\not\equiv73\pmod {10},
\quad 3\not\equiv47\pmod {10},
\quad 5\not\equiv29\pmod {10},
\]
\[
7\not\equiv19\pmod {10},
\quad 11\not\equiv13\pmod {10}.
\]
Explicitly, the corresponding pairs of final digits are \((2,3),(3,7),(5,9),(7,9),(1,3)\).

We next show that every positive \(d\le 2025\) is coprime to at least one of those five products. Suppose, to the contrary, that \(d\) were not coprime to any of them. Since each product consists of two distinct primes, non-coprimality with it says that at least one of its two prime factors divides \(d\). Thus we could choose primes
\[
r_1\in\{2,73\},\quad
r_2\in\{3,47\},\quad
r_3\in\{5,29\},\quad
r_4\in\{7,19\},\quad
r_5\in\{11,13\}
\]
such that every \(r_j\) divides \(d\).

All ten primes displayed in the five pairs are distinct, so the selected primes \(r_1,\ldots,r_5\) are distinct and hence pairwise coprime. Consequently their product divides \(d\). Since \(d>0\), this gives
\[
d\ge r_1r_2r_3r_4r_5.
\]
Each selected prime is at least the smaller member of its pair, and therefore
\[
r_1r_2r_3r_4r_5
 \ge 2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11
 =2310.
\]
It would follow that \(d\ge2310\), contrary to \(d\le2025\). We have therefore established the five-way alternative
\[
\gcd(d,146)=1,
\quad\text{or}\quad
\gcd(d,141)=1,
\quad\text{or}\quad
\gcd(d,145)=1,
\quad\text{or}\quad
\gcd(d,133)=1,
\quad\text{or}\quad
\gcd(d,143)=1.
\]

Assume now, for contradiction, that \(a,d\) satisfy the conjectured conditions and that every \(a+id\), for \(0\le i<150\), is lopsided. Choose from the five pairs above a pair \((p,q)\) for which
\[
\gcd(d,pq)=1;
\]
such a pair exists by the preceding argument. Apply the modular hitting lemma with \(m=pq\). It supplies an integer \(i\) such that
\[
0\le i<pq
\quad\text{and}\quad
pq\mid a+id.
\]
For each of the five possible choices, \(pq\le150\), so \(i<pq\le150\), hence \(0\le i<150\). Thus \(a+id\) is one of the 150 terms that were assumed to be lopsided.

On the other hand, \(pq\mid a+id\) implies that both primes \(p\) and \(q\) divide \(a+id\). The term is certainly greater than 1, because
\[
a+id\ge a\ge2.
\]
Therefore \(p\) and \(q\) are two genuine prime divisors of this term. But, by construction of the five pairs, \(p\not\equiv q\pmod {10}\). Hence these two prime divisors have different final decimal digits, so \(a+id\) is not lopsided. This contradicts the assumption that all 150 progression terms are lopsided.

For completeness, the final contradiction splits into exactly the following five possible cases:

* If \(\gcd(d,146)=1\), some term with index \(i<146\) is divisible by both \(2\) and \(73\), whose final digits are 2 and 3.
* If \(\gcd(d,141)=1\), some term with index \(i<141\) is divisible by both \(3\) and \(47\), whose final digits are 3 and 7.
* If \(\gcd(d,145)=1\), some term with index \(i<145\) is divisible by both \(5\) and \(29\), whose final digits are 5 and 9.
* If \(\gcd(d,133)=1\), some term with index \(i<133\) is divisible by both \(7\) and \(19\), whose final digits are 7 and 9.
* If \(\gcd(d,143)=1\), some term with index \(i<143\) is divisible by both \(11\) and \(13\), whose final digits are 1 and 3.

Every case produces a non-lopsided term among the first 150 terms. Thus no such \(a\) and \(d\) exist, and the stated conjecture is false.
